qs.q: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus develops non-infective endocarditis characterized by vegetations affecting both sides of the mitral valve. What is this specific condition called?
qs.e: Libman-Sacks endocarditis is associated with SLE and affects both sides of the mitral valve. Marantic endocarditis is typically seen in patients with malignancy or debilitating illness.

faq.a: They consist solely of unorganised platelets and fibrin without a robust inflammatory reaction to anchor them firmly to the valve leaflet.
faq.q: Why do non-infective vegetations embolise more easily than infective ones?

faq.a: Unlike infective vegetations which form on the flow surface, Libman-Sacks lesions develop on both flow and non-flow surfaces, including valve undersurfaces.
faq.q: Where are Libman-Sacks vegetations located on the heart valve?

faq.a: Warfarin has high failure rates in malignancy-associated thrombosis; heparin-based anticoagulants provide better suppression of tumor-related thrombin generation.
faq.q: Why is warfarin often avoided in cancer-associated non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis?

exam: A wasted patient with adenocarcinoma presents with a dense hemiplegia; cardiac exam reveals a soft systolic murmur. What is the diagnosis and pathophysiology? — Non-bacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis; hypercoagulability from tumor-derived tissue factor causes sterile platelet-fibrin deposition, which easily fragments and embolises.

How does the anatomical distribution of Libman-Sacks endocarditis differ from infective endocarditis? — Libman-Sacks lesions appear on both sides of the valve leaflets (flow and non-flow surfaces) and valve pocket undersurfaces, whereas infective vegetations typically adhere strictly to the flow surface.

What steps ensure blood cultures are truly negative before concluding endocarditis is non-infective? — Draw at least three sets of blood cultures spaced over time before administering antibiotics, hold cultures for prolonged incubation, and perform serology for fastidious organisms like Coxiella and Bartonella.

Why are direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) avoided in a patient with NBTE caused by antiphospholipid syndrome? — High-quality clinical trials showed higher rates of recurrent arterial thromboembolic events with DOACs compared to low-molecular-weight heparin and target-adjusted warfarin in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome.

How do you distinguish acute rheumatic endocarditis verrucae from marantic endocarditis on macroscopic pathology? — Rheumatic verrucae are tiny, firm, wart-like sterile beads strictly along the lines of valve closure; marantic vegetations are larger, irregular, softer, more friable, and loosely attached.

A patient with known Libman-Sacks endocarditis develops high fever and rigors. What is the immediate concern? — Secondary bacterial seeding of the sterile vegetation converting non-infective endocarditis into secondary infective endocarditis.

Why can a normal transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) never safely rule out non-infective endocarditis? — TTE has low sensitivity for masses under 5 mm; non-infective vegetations are frequently small and flat, demanding transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE) for exclusion.
ai.title: Non-Infective Endocarditis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Non-infective endocarditis involves sterile platelet and fibrin thrombi forming on heart valves without microorganism invasion. It arises primarily from hypercoagulable states, systemic lupus erythematosus, or acute rheumatic fever. Embolic strokes and valvular destruction represent the greatest immediate threats to survival.

b: Vegetations are sterile, bland, and lack bacterial colonies or heavy neutrophil infiltrates.
They are typically easily dislodged because they lack destructive inflammatory anchoring into valve tissue.
Clinical diagnosis requires exclusion of infective endocarditis with persistently negative blood cultures.
sections.p: Non-infective endocarditis is the deposition of sterile platelet-fibrin vegetations on cardiac valves in the absence of bloodstream infection. Diagnosis rests on detecting valvular masses on echocardiography alongside negative blood cultures and an identifiable predisposing prothrombotic or autoimmune disease.

b: Mild: Small, asymptomatic, non-destructive verrucae detected incidentally on imaging.
Moderate: Moderate-sized vegetations causing new or changing murmurs without hemodynamic instability.
Severe: Large mobile vegetations over 10 mm, systemic embolisation (cerebral, renal, splenic), or acute valvular regurgitation with heart failure.
sections.p: There is no formal numerical staging system; severity is graded by valve dysfunction, vegetation burden, and embolic complications.

b: Acute rheumatic fever: Sterile, small, warty verrucae along lines of valve closure triggered by post-streptococcal molecular mimicry.
Hypercoagulable and malignant states (Marantic): Mucinous adenocarcinomas (pancreas, lung, stomach) and advanced HIV wasting producing prothrombotic tissue factor.
Systemic lupus erythematosus (Libman-Sacks): Immune complex deposition on both valve surfaces, especially mitral and aortic.
Antiphospholipid syndrome: Primary or secondary hypercoagulability causing sterile platelet aggregates on injured endothelium.
Severe chronic wasting: Advanced tuberculosis, severe malnutrition, or end-stage renal disease promoting low-grade disseminated intravascular coagulation.
sections.p: In low-resource and high-burden settings, underlying systemic inflammatory and hypercoagulable conditions drive sterile vegetation formation.

b: Sudden focal neurological deficits from embolic stroke, often in a young lupus patient or wasted cancer patient.
New or changing regurgitant heart murmur, most commonly mitral or aortic, though murmurs can be soft or absent.
Absence of fever, chills, or classical infective peripheral stigmata (no Osler nodes or Janeway lesions).
Signs of underlying illness: Malar rash, joint pains, profound cachexia, or unexplained weight loss.
sections.p: The disease is notoriously clinically silent until an embolic catastrophe occurs or the underlying chronic disease decompensates.

t.a: Serial blood cultures (at least three sets before antibiotics)
t.b: Differentiates from infective endocarditis; persistently negative cultures support non-infective endocarditis.
Screens for vegetations and valvular regurgitation; if negative but suspicion is high, proceed to transoesophageal imaging.
Identifies small, broad-based, or multiple vegetations missed on TTE; essential before confirming sterile status.

t.a: Full blood count and peripheral film
t.b: Detects cytopenias in lupus, leukocytosis in acute rheumatic fever, or microangiopathic features in hypercoagulability.
Assesses systemic inflammation; markedly raised in active rheumatic fever and autoimmune flares.
Diagnoses underlying systemic lupus erythematosus as the cause of Libman-Sacks lesions.
Identifies secondary or primary antiphospholipid syndrome driving valve thrombi.
Low-resource search for primary occult malignancy, pulmonary tuberculosis, or systemic embolic infarctions.

b: Ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack due to embolisation into cerebral circulation.
Acute heart failure from rapid valve destruction or severe leaflet retraction.
Secondary bacterial colonisation: Transient bacteremia seeds sterile vegetations, transforming NBTE into acute infective endocarditis.
Mesenteric, splenic, or renal infarction presenting with acute severe abdominal or flank pain.
sections.p: Complications relate directly to fragmentation of the friable vegetations and valvular insufficiency.

b: Anticoagulation: Unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin is preferred over vitamin K antagonists in malignancy-associated NBTE due to superior efficacy.
Direct oral anticoagulants are generally avoided in antiphospholipid syndrome due to higher arterial thrombosis rates.
Treat the driver: Systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressants (such as hydroxychloroquine) for active lupus; chemotherapy or palliation for underlying malignancy.
Rheumatic fever therapy: Benzathine penicillin eradicates persistent streptococcal carriage, paired with anti-inflammatory therapy.
Avoid empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics once true sterile status is reliably confirmed, preventing unnecessary drug toxicity and resistance.
Surgical intervention: Valve repair or replacement reserved for severe acute regurgitation, refractory heart failure, or large persistent mobile vegetations.
sections.p: Management centers on controlling the underlying systemic driver and preventing catastrophic arterial thromboembolism.

b: Serial echocardiography at regular intervals to monitor vegetation regression and progressive valvular dysfunction.
Secondary prophylaxis with intramuscular benzathine penicillin every 3 to 4 weeks if acute rheumatic fever was the cause.
Strict adherence to cancer screening or autoimmune immunosuppression to prevent recurrent prothrombotic surges.
Prompt medical review for any sudden neurological deficit, chest pain, or unheralded fever.
sections.p: Long-term care aims to suppress the driving inflammatory state and ensure lifelong secondary prophylaxis when indicated.

b: Infective endocarditis: Presents with fever, raised inflammatory markers, positive blood cultures, and tissue destruction.
Culture-negative infective endocarditis: Caused by fastidious organisms (Brucella, Coxiella) or prior antibiotics; requires serology.
Atrial myxoma: Produces systemic emboli and constitutional symptoms, but mass is intracavitary and usually attached to fossa ovalis.
Degenerative calcific aortic valve disease: Causes murmurs in elderly individuals; lacks friable, mobile, sterile verrucae.
sections.p: Clinical overlap is high with other causes of valvular vegetations and embolic phenomena.

b: TTE false negatives: Vegetations smaller than 5 mm are frequently missed; negative TTE never excludes the condition.
Blood cultures taken after empiric antibiotics: Sterilises infective endocarditis, creating false appearance of sterile NBTE.
Lupus anticoagulant testing: Prolonged clotting times can mislead clinicians to expect bleeding, yet patients are prothrombotic.
Elevated inflammatory markers: High ESR or CRP in advanced cancer or lupus mimics active bacterial infection.
sections.p: Diagnostic tests can generate false reassurance or misdirection during evaluation.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden weakness, facial droop, or speech difficulty suggesting embolic stroke.
Sudden-onset severe breathlessness or orthopnea indicating acute pulmonary edema.
Severe cold, painful, or pale limb pointing to acute peripheral arterial occlusion.
New-onset fever in a patient with known non-infective vegetations.
